title: AUD U1·W3 — Internal Control & Fraud in the Audit (CPA Core · from CMA m5/m12)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — MBG's transaction registry, seen by the auditor

CMA months 5 and 12 built MBG's controls — segregation of duties and the VERIFIED/POSTED/FLAGGED transaction registry. AUD looks at those same controls from outside: the auditor must understand internal control, decide whether to rely on it, and stay alert to fraud, including management's ability to override the very controls that look strong on paper.

Understanding and testing internal control

On every audit, the auditor must obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit — all five COSO components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring. Understanding is required even if the auditor does not plan to rely on controls.

To rely on controls (assess control risk below maximum and reduce substantive testing), the auditor must test their operating effectiveness with tests of controls. Tests of controls ask "did the control operate?"; substantive procedures ask "is the balance correct?" If controls are ineffective or the auditor chooses not to rely on them, control risk is high and substantive testing increases (the model from last week).

The integrated audit (SOX)

For issuers (public companies), Sarbanes-Oxley §404 and PCAOB standards require an integrated audit: the auditor opines on both the financial statements and the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). A material weakness (a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement not being prevented or detected) yields an adverse ICFR opinion. A private company like MBG is not subject to §404, but the same control concepts drive the financial-statement audit.

Fraud and professional skepticism (AU-C 240)

Two fraud types: fraudulent financial reporting (intentional misstatement to deceive users) and misappropriation of assets (theft). The fraud triangle from CMA month 12 — pressure, opportunity, rationalization — drives the auditor's risk assessment. Required procedures include an engagement-team brainstorming about how fraud could occur, inquiries of management and others, and a presumption that improper revenue recognition is a fraud risk.

Critically, the auditor must always address the risk of management override of controls — even strong controls can be overridden by those who design them. Required responses include testing journal entries (especially nonstandard, period-end, and round-dollar entries), reviewing accounting estimates for bias, and evaluating significant unusual transactions. Professional skepticism means not accepting evidence at face value just because management seems honest.

The five components and control activities

Each COSO component does specific work. The control environment is the tone at the top — integrity, board oversight, competence. Risk assessment is management’s own identification of risks to reporting. Control activities are the policies that address those risks: authorization, segregation of duties (separating authorization, recording, and custody), physical controls over assets and records, reconciliations, and performance reviews. Information and communication captures and shares the data that make controls run, and monitoring evaluates whether controls keep working over time. MBG’s segregation of duties is a control activity; its transaction registry is part of information and communication and supports monitoring.

Design, implementation, and walkthroughs

Understanding control is not one question but three. The auditor evaluates whether a control is designed effectively (would it prevent or detect a misstatement?) and whether it has been implemented (does it actually exist and operate?) — assessed through inquiry combined with observation, inspection, or a walkthrough that traces one transaction from origination through the records. Only when the auditor intends to rely on a control does it additionally test operating effectiveness over the period. Design-and-implementation work is required on every audit; operating-effectiveness testing is required only for reliance (and, for issuers, for the ICFR opinion).

Deficiencies and required communications

Control problems are graded by severity. A control deficiency exists when a control does not let management or employees prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis. A significant deficiency is important enough to merit the attention of those charged with governance. A material weakness is the most severe — a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected — and, for an issuer, forces an adverse ICFR opinion. The auditor must communicate significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in writing to those charged with governance, and that communication is required even if the deficiencies were remediated during the year.

The inherent limitations of any control system

No system of internal control gives absolute assurance, and the exam tests why. Management override lets those who design the controls bypass them; collusion between two or more people defeats segregation of duties; human error and faulty judgment cause breakdowns; and cost-benefit constraints mean management will not control immaterial risks. These limitations are precisely why an auditor cannot rely on controls alone and must always perform some substantive procedures, and why even a clean ICFR opinion is reasonable, not absolute, assurance. They also explain the standing requirement to address management override regardless of how strong the controls appear.

IT controls, service organizations, and illegal acts

Most controls today are embedded in systems. IT general controls (ITGCs) — over access and security, program change management, and computer operations — underpin the application controls (edit checks, validations, automated reconciliations) the auditor may rely on; weak ITGCs can undermine otherwise sound application controls. When a client outsources a process (payroll, hosting) to a service organization, the auditor obtains a SOC 1 report from the service auditor: a type 1 covers design at a point in time, a type 2 covers operating effectiveness over a period, and only a type 2 supports reliance on those controls. Finally, the auditor considers laws and regulations: noncompliance with a direct effect on the statements is audited like any other misstatement, and the auditor responds to identified or suspected noncompliance by evaluating the effect and communicating to the appropriate level — escalating to those charged with governance when senior management is involved.

Communicating and documenting fraud findings

When the auditor identifies fraud or a suspicion of it, the communication path depends on who is involved and how material it is. Any fraud involving senior management, or fraud that causes a material misstatement, is communicated to those charged with governance; even immaterial fraud by an employee is reported to the appropriate level of management. The auditor’s normal duty of confidentiality may yield to a duty to disclose outside the entity in limited circumstances (a successor auditor with client consent, a subpoena, a regulator). Throughout, the auditor maintains professional skepticism and documents the fraud risk assessment, the brainstorming, the responses, and the basis for conclusions — the work that lets a later reviewer confirm the override and revenue-recognition risks were genuinely addressed rather than assumed away. If the risk is so severe that the auditor can no longer rely on management’s representations, withdrawal from the engagement may be the only appropriate response.

CMA bridge

CMA framed segregation of duties and the transaction registry as fraud prevention (denying opportunity); AUD adds the auditor's detection responsibility — test the controls, and never assume they cannot be overridden from the top.

Practice and recap

  1. Obtain an understanding of all five COSO components on every audit.
  2. To rely on controls, test their operating effectiveness; otherwise increase substantive testing.
  3. For issuers, perform an integrated audit of ICFR; a material weakness → adverse ICFR opinion.
  4. Assess fraud risk (triangle), presume revenue-recognition fraud, and always address management override by testing journal entries.

Recap: the auditor understands internal control on every engagement and tests it only to rely on it; issuers get an integrated ICFR audit; and fraud work — brainstorming, the revenue-recognition presumption, and journal-entry testing for management override — runs on professional skepticism.

questions.q: On every audit, the auditor must obtain an understanding of internal control:
choices: Always, covering all five COSO components
questions.explain: Understanding all five COSO components is required on every audit, regardless of reliance.

questions.q: To assess control risk below maximum and rely on a control, the auditor must:
choices: Test its operating effectiveness (tests of controls)
questions.explain: Reliance requires tests of controls demonstrating operating effectiveness.

questions.q: An integrated audit under SOX §404 applies to:
questions.explain: SOX §404 integrated ICFR audits are required for issuers.

questions.q: A material weakness in ICFR results in which opinion on internal control?
questions.explain: A material weakness yields an adverse opinion on ICFR.

questions.q: Which fraud risk is presumed on every financial-statement audit?
questions.explain: AU-C 240 presumes a risk of improper revenue recognition (and requires addressing management override).

questions.q: The primary required response to the risk of management override of controls is to:
choices: Test journal entries and review estimates for bias
questions.explain: Testing journal entries (nonstandard/period-end/round-dollar) and reviewing estimates addresses override risk.

questions.q: A test of controls differs from a substantive procedure because it:
choices: Evaluates whether a control operated effectively
questions.explain: Tests of controls assess operating effectiveness; substantive procedures detect misstatements in balances.
